prompt.context: Our client is a major US television network that is trying to figure out how much to bid for the 2018 Winter Olympics and has brought you in to help them figure out the right bid. The Winter Olympics are a huge deal and will require a significant amount of capital to secure the rights. Before their network bids on the Winter Olympics, they'd like to make sure that they've considered all the right things.
prompt.question: How much should the network bid for the 2018 Winter Olympics broadcasting rights?

clarifying_info.q: What is the schedule for the Winter Olympics broadcast?
clarifying_info.a: 16 days total. Day 1 (Friday): Opening Ceremonies – 3 hours of programming from 8-11 PM. Days 2-15: Games – 10 hours/day (Weekdays: 9-12, 2-5, 7-11; Weekends: 11 AM – 9 PM). Day 16 (Saturday): Closing Ceremonies – 3 hours from 8-11 PM.

No subscription revenue. The network can keep 100% of advertising revenue. Ad rates are $400K per 30-second ad for prime time (M-F 7-11 PM and all weekend) and $200K per ad for non-prime time. Market research shows you can include no more than 10 minutes of advertising per hour.
Total direct costs are $428M. There is also an opportunity cost of $1M per hour of programming aired. There is a 6-year lag between bidding and receipt of revenue, with a WACC of 12%.

framework: Revenues: Calculate total advertising revenue across all programming windows (prime time vs. non-prime time, weekdays vs. weekends, opening/closing ceremonies)
Costs: Identify three cost components – direct production costs, opportunity costs (foregone programming revenue), and time value of money (discount revenues back to present using WACC)
NPV: Combine revenues and all costs to determine the financial value of the bid
Qualitative / intangible factors: Consider non-financial benefits that could justify a higher bid (new viewers, network prestige, cross-promotion, product tie-ins)
Recommendation: Synthesize NPV with qualitative factors to recommend a bid amount, with justification for any deviation from pure NPV

questions.prompt: Calculate the total advertising revenue from broadcasting the Winter Olympics.
questions.guidance: Candidate must segment programming into four buckets and calculate ad slots per bucket. Key insight: 10 min/hr of ads = 20 slots/hr (each slot is 30 seconds). Prime time = M-F 7-11 PM and all weekend hours.

math.setup: Segment into: (1) Weekday prime time, (2) Weekday non-prime time, (3) Weekend, (4) Opening/Closing ceremonies. For each: days x hours/day x 10 min ads/hr x 2 slots/min x rate/slot.
steps: Weekday prime time (M-F, 7-11 PM = 4 hrs, 10 days): 10 days x 4 hrs x 10 min/hr x 2 slots/min x $400K = $320M
Weekday non-prime time (M-F, 9-12 and 2-5 = 6 hrs, 10 days): 10 days x 6 hrs x 10 min/hr x 2 slots/min x $200K = $240M
Weekend (Sat/Sun of Days 2-15 = 4 weekend days, 10 hrs each, all prime time): 4 days x 10 hrs x 10 min/hr x 2 slots/min x $400K = $320M
Opening/Closing Ceremonies (2 days x 3 hrs, prime time): 2 days x 3 hrs x 10 min/hr x 2 slots/min x $400K = $48M

questions.prompt: Factoring in all costs, what is the NPV of the Olympics broadcast rights? Is this a good investment?
questions.guidance: Candidate must apply three cost types: (1) direct costs $428M, (2) opportunity costs based on hours of programming, (3) time value – use Rule of 72 to discount future revenues. Strong candidates will note the Rule of 72 shortcut: 72 / 12% WACC = 6 years to double, so with a 6-year lag, all net cash flows are halved.

math.setup: NPV = (Revenue - Direct Costs - Opportunity Costs) / 2 [per Rule of 72 at 12% WACC over 6 years]
steps: Opportunity cost: (2 ceremony days x 3 hrs x $1M/hr) + (14 game days x 10 hrs x $1M/hr) = $6M + $140M = $146M
Pre-discount net: $928M - $428M direct costs - $146M opportunity cost = $354M
Rule of 72: 72 / 12% = 6 years to double; since revenue received 6 years out, halve the net cash flow
math.answer: NPV = $177M; yes, the investment has positive NPV

brainstorming.prompt: Beyond the NPV figure of $177M, what intangible factors could influence how high the network should bid?

categories.name: Audience & Brand
ideas: Access to new viewers who do not normally watch the network
Increased brand prestige and recognition from hosting a major global event
Halo effect on other programming that follows the Olympics

categories.name: Cross-Promotion & Programming
ideas: Use Olympic air time to promote other network shows and boost their ratings
Build multi-year audience relationships that benefit future programming cycles

categories.name: Supplemental Revenue
ideas: Product tie-ins and sponsorship deals with Olympic-themed brands
Digital/streaming rights and ancillary revenue streams

categories.name: Competitive / Game Theory
ideas: Risk of a competitor winning the rights and gaining a strategic audience advantage
Need to consider other bidders' likely bids and not just own NPV
Long-term rights deals may include future Olympics packages

categories.name: Risks
ideas: Uncertain viewership – poor athletic performance or lack of star athletes could reduce ratings
Geopolitical issues with the host country affecting viewership or advertiser sentiment

recommendation: The network should bid approximately $200M for the 2018 Winter Olympics broadcasting rights
The pure financial NPV is $177M, but intangible benefits – new viewer acquisition, cross-promotional value, and network prestige – justify a modest premium above the NPV figure
A bid in the range of $177M–$220M is defensible; significant deviation in either direction requires strong justification
risks: Actual viewership may fall short of projections, reducing ad revenue below $928M
Competitor bids could far exceed NPV, suggesting rivals place higher value on intangibles
Cost overruns in production could erode the NPV margin
next_steps: Conduct scenario analysis on ad revenue sensitivity to viewership ratings
Gather competitive intelligence on other networks' bidding strategies
Quantify the cross-promotional value of air time to support a bid above $177M
